title: A Story of Halves
author: Text Savvy
summary: This installment of a math-as-language curriculum series introduces fractions as a naming system, using halves to extend students' intuitions built around whole numbers. The denominator is framed as a unit-of-measure name rather than a procedural directive: /2 means 'halves' in the same way that /1 means 'wholes.' The author advocates for teaching mathematics as a language — building conceptual meaning before introducing notation or procedure. A concept like factorial should conjure 'arrangements of a fixed set' before it invokes multiplication steps. The number line is used proprioceptively (running a finger across it) to let students feel equivalence between 1 whole and 2 halves. The core claim: students are supported when they understand mathematics as a set of ideas that lead to procedures, rather than as a set of procedures to memorize.
points: The denominator in a fraction is a unit-of-measure name, not a procedural directive: /2 means 'halves' just as /1 means 'wholes.'
Teaching math as a language means building conceptual meaning before notation — it should mean something before you write or draw it.
Starting with a procedural definition of a mathematical concept subtly skips the grounding 'about-ness': what is this about, and how do we talk about it?
Running a finger across the number line lets students feel the equivalence of 1 whole and 2 halves proprioceptively, reinforcing the continuousness of fraction measurement.
Students are supported when they understand mathematics as ideas that lead to procedures, not as procedures to memorize before the ideas are established.
quotes: The denominator '1' is the name for the unit of measure we call 'wholes' and the denominator '2' is the name for the unit of measure we call 'halves.'
The latter is a proceduralization of a meaning taught before the meaning itself.
Whenever I make the case for math to be taught 'as a language,' it should mean something to you before you write or draw something next.
To start with a procedural definition of some mathematical concept is to subtly skip over the grounding 'about-ness' of the concept: what is this about? and how do we talk about it?
Students are supported well in their mathematics learning when they are able to know and talk about mathematics as a set of ideas that lead to certain procedures — not as a set of procedures.
